set.descent_text: Parties go down the way they came up. From the summit they follow the ridge back to the Denali Pass traverse and drop to high camp, then continue down to the camp near 14,000 feet, where many leave food and fuel for the return. From there the route follows the boot track down the Kahiltna Glacier to the airstrip, with crevasses along the lower glacier, and flights return to Talkeetna. After the climb, teams check out with the park ranger station in Talkeetna.
set.approach: Climbers fly by ski plane from Talkeetna to the Kahiltna Glacier landing, a little over 7,000 feet on the southeast fork, and the route starts there. Every independent climber must register with the park before the climb, and the whole team attends an orientation at the Talkeetna ranger station and signs the permit; air taxis will not fly a team in until that is done. From the landing a boot track leads up the Kahiltna Glacier to the first camp near the confluence with the northeast fork, with crevasses to rope up for from the start.

review.notes: Approach: Alpine Institute (ski plane from Talkeetna, Kahiltna landing ~7,300; camp 1 at NE Fork confluence), MP WB (7,200 start), MP West Rib (boot track, 7,800 ABC, NE Fork; descent via WB camps to airstrip, 14k cache for descent), NPS FAQ (registration, orientation, check-out). Elevation stated only as 'a little over 7,000' since sources give 7,200/7,300. Descent route is inferred from West Rib page + reversal; medium.

set.descent_text: The Sultana Ridge is itself the usual descent for Foraker, so parties reverse the climb. From the high camp they work back along the long ridge to Mount Crosson, cross over its summit again and descend to the Kahiltna Glacier. The first day down aims to reach Crosson, which makes for a long, tiring retreat over cornices and crevasses; a bush pilot then flies the party back to Talkeetna from the glacier.
set.approach: Parties fly by ski plane from Talkeetna to the southeast fork of the Kahiltna Glacier, then cross the glacier to an advanced base camp at the foot of Mount Crosson. The route begins with the climb up Crosson's ridge. Everyone must register with the park service and attend the Talkeetna orientation before flying in. Crevasses are present on the glacier approach.

review.notes: MP: standard descent for all Foraker routes, same start as Denali routes. Alpine Institute: retrace over Crosson to Kahiltna, bush pilot flies out. Mountain Trip: southeast fork landing, ABC at base of Crosson, descent day 1 aims for Crosson, then to the glacier and airstrip.

set.approach: The usual access is an air taxi from Talkeetna onto the Kahiltna Glacier, with park registration done beforehand at the Talkeetna mountaineering headquarters. The ridge is reached from the head of the glacier near the upper West Buttress camps, taking the easiest line up from the glacier; a side trip over Mt. Capps, a minor bump joining the West Buttress ridge to the Dome, can be added. There are crevasses at the base of the ridge and on the ridge itself.

review.notes: MP route + MP area page (air taxi, registration). No descent source.

set.descent_text: Descend the line of ascent. The ridge is moderately exposed, and the talus and fourth-class rock field below it can be slippery, so take care on the way down to the campsite at the base.
set.approach: This is a long overland trip from Wonder Lake on the park road: the approach reaches the mountain by way of McGonagall Pass or Oastler Pass, and the base of the route lies at the lower left as seen from Oastler Pass, where a tundra and rock campsite sits. Any of several lines up the apron gains the ridge. Registration with the park mountaineering office in Talkeetna is required before climbing.

review.notes: MP route: start at lower left from Oastler Pass, descend the line of ascent. MP area: bus to Wonder Lake and hike into McGonagall or Oastler Pass. NPS blog: road closed past East Fork Toklat (slump). Mileage omitted. Medium: single route page.

set.descent_text: The couloir is also the way down for other routes on the peak, so descend it from the upper slopes. It is steep, and the snow can be poor after warm weather. The base is reached across the crevasse field east of the couloir.
set.approach: From the Mountain House area, travel north near the middle of the Ruth Glacier, the safest line, and follow it around east and then south into the gorge, continuing along beneath Barrill's east face until you stand due east of the Japanese Couloir, then turn west. That spot usually gives the simplest, safest crossing of the crevasses to the foot of the peak. The approach can be short, depending on where base camp is, but finding a route through the crevasses to the base can take some work. Register with the Talkeetna mountaineering headquarters before climbing in the park.

review.notes: MP area page: approach and crevasse crossing, warm-weather caution. Alpine Institute: approach short, crevasse route-finding. MP Cobra Pillar: descend via the Japanese Couloir. Descent method not stated (no rappel count).

set.approach: Access is by charter flight to the Klutlan Glacier, where crevasse falls and accidents have been frequent, so travel roped and carefully. From the landing, climb the glacier to the left of a broken rib of seracs, where a wind-loaded ramp can provide the best snow bridges, to a good camp spot. Above it the way continues up a heavily crevassed, glaciated bowl with some avalanche danger to reach the large caldera plateau. From the rim, Mount Churchill's southeast ridge starts a flat mile away, while Mount Bona needs a longer traverse of the plateau.

review.notes: MP route + area page (charter flight in). Heights and distances omitted (single source). No descent source.

set.approach: Access is by charter flight to a landing zone on the Nabesna Glacier. Glacier travel to the south slope is fairly straightforward by Wrangell standards, and a second camp can be made higher on the glacier. The same landing zone serves Mount Wrangell, whose low-angle glaciers hold very large crevasses, so take crevasse precautions.

review.notes: MP route + area page (fly in). Elevations omitted. No descent source.

set.approach: The approach comes from the west along the Huluhulu River, then follows Esetuk Creek past several forks. The ground is wet tundra giving way to talus and boulder slopes where snow lingers into June, and the travel is slow and tedious. Stay out of the creek bed by side-hilling on higher ground, which is a challenge during early-season melt. Go over the Esetuk Glacier close to its terminus to get to the root of the peak, then work up a steep boulder field to a higher point on the ridge, where the terrain turns to snow. In June and July the daylight lasts around the clock.

review.notes: Single MP page. No descent source.

set.approach: The couloir is normally entered from above: parties climb the South Gully from the Eklutna Lake trailhead by way of the Twin Peaks trail, then rappel in at the entrance from slung rock horns or pitons. The terrain is steep snow and very complex avalanche terrain, so check the local avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: MP route + area page (access via Eklutna Lake Road and Twin Peaks trail). Single-source on the rappel entry. No descent source.

set.approach: Most parties start at the Eklutna Lake trailhead, take the Twin Peaks trail and climb the south side of the mountain to the top of the couloir. The other option is a long, bushy approach from Old Glenn, which makes a typically miserable day. The line is steep, narrow and avalanche-prone, so it is best entered in very stable conditions after studying the map and the snow.

review.notes: Single MP page. No descent source.

set.approach: Park at the Glen Alps trailhead and follow Powerline Pass to the base of the main couloir on Ptarmigan's north face. This wide couloir is also the access to many other routes on the face. Avalanches occur in it, so check conditions before committing.

review.notes: MP area + route page. Time omitted. No descent source (page says the couloir can be taken to the ridge and summit).

set.approach: Scott Peak rises steeply above the head of the Sunset Glacier. Parties reach the Thorofare River gravel bar from the Eielson Visitor Center area on the park road (check current road and bus status), then follow the river toward the Sunset Glacier basin, which needs a river crossing that can be difficult on warm days and after rain. Overnight use of this backcountry unit needs a park permit, and the unit has a quota. Once on the Sunset Glacier, the route follows it to its upper basin.

review.notes: NPS Unit 12 page: access from Eielson / Thorofare Pass, Thorofare gravel bar, river crossing, quota permit, Scott Peak above head of Sunset Glacier. MP: follow glacier to upper basin. Bus/road status currently disrupted; not stated. No descent source.

ak_arctic_national_wildlife_refuge_mt_ch.skip_reason: Only source is one route page with a multi-day approach noted but no landing, drainage or descent; nothing supports a paragraph.

ak_denali_muldrow_glacier.skip_reason: The park says the Muldrow is not currently recommended after the 2021 glacier surge, and no source describes the approach or descent in a way that is reliable now.

ak_radio_control_tower_standard_route_no.skip_reason: No readable source: the only accounts are a browser-only SummitPost page and a JavaScript-gated guide site.

ak_o_malley_peak_3_thunderbolt_lightenin.skip_reason: Only source is one route page describing a ski descent (above Black Lake); no trailhead, approach or climbing descent is stated.
